chunks: Reflections and why they matter. The question: What are reflections? Why do I care about them?
A reflection is part of a signal bouncing back when it meets a change in impedance. A wave on a line sees the line's characteristic impedance.
If it reaches something different, such as the end of the line or a connector, part goes on and part comes back. This causes ringing, overshoot and false edges.
Think of an ocean wave arriving at a shore. A gently sloping beach absorbs the wave and almost nothing returns. A solid sea wall throws the wave straight back.
The beach is a load matched to the line. The wall is an open end. In between you get a partial reflection.
On a real line the bounced wave can bounce again at the driver, so it keeps going back and forth.
Each diagonal is a wave crossing the line in one delay, labelled with its amplitude.
At the open load the wave reflects unchanged ( L equals plus 1 ), so the load voltage jumps by 2 times 2. 75 equals 5. 5 volts. At the source it reflects with S equals -0.
67 , so the next wave is minus 1. 83 volts, which pulls the load voltage down to 1. 83 volts. The amplitude shrinks by 0. 67 per round trip and the voltage converges to 3.
3 volts.
Impedance: how strongly a part opposes current when a signal is applied.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the impedance a wave sees as it travels along the line ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Reflection coefficient ( ): the fraction of the arriving wave that bounces back, (Z L minus Z 0) over (Z L plus Z 0) .
Ringing: the repeated up-and-down wiggle caused by waves bouncing back and forth ("Ringing").
A 50 ohms line ends in a 100 ohms load. The reflection coefficient is (100 - 50) / (100 + 50) = 1/3, so one third of the arriving wave comes back.
A matched 50 ohms load gives zero reflection. An open end gives +1, so all of it comes back. Now drive that line from 3. 3 volts through 10 ohms, with the far end open.
The first wave is 2. 75 volts. At the open end it reflects completely and adds to itself, so the far end jumps to 5. 5 volts.
The reflected wave then returns to the driver and bounces again. That is the whole idea: a change in impedance sends part of the wave back.
"A reflection is the part of a wave that bounces back at an impedance change.
The reflected fraction is equals (Z L-Z 0) over (Z L plus Z 0) : +1 for an open, minus 1 for a short, zero when the load equals Z 0 .
If the source isn't matched either, the wave bounces back and forth and you see ringing and overshoot. I care because it can push a 3. 3 volts line to 5.
5 volts, cause false clock edges, close the eye and radiate EMI. You fix it by matching impedances and terminating."
